1a:
**Sub-item 1a — UTF-8 supports more character sets than ASCII**

Award credit (no deduct) only when the answer makes an explicit comparative claim about character coverage that puts **both** encodings side by side — e.g., "ASCII covers only 128 code points while UTF-8 covers all of Unicode," so the "more than" relation is actually asserted and supported. What matters is that the answer somewhere characterizes what characters/bytes each encoding can actually represent; it does not matter whether the answer also recommends keeping headers ASCII-only or takes any particular position on the fix. An answer satisfies this equally when the comparison is delivered inside the decode discussion: if, in explaining that `.decode('ascii')` fails on non-ASCII bytes, the answer conveys in that same breath that such characters lie outside ASCII's repertoire but are representable/handled by UTF-8, the breadth point is considered made and no deduction applies.

Deduct the point when the answer speaks to only one encoding's coverage (an ASCII-limitation-only remark, or a UTF-8-covers-Unicode remark, with nothing said about the other), when the breadth difference is merely inferable from separate, uncompared statements rather than asserted as a comparison, or when the answer argues purely from protocol/standards compliance (e.g., "HTTP headers must be ASCII per the spec, so encode as ASCII") without ever characterizing what characters each encoding can represent.
1b:
No_deduct only when the answer explicitly invokes the ASCII codec as the thing that fails — e.g. `.decode('ascii')`, `codecs.decode(..., 'ascii')`, `str(b, 'ascii')`, or prose that names the ascii codec/decoder — *and* affirmatively states that this raises a concrete, named error on data outside ASCII, identifying the exception (UnicodeDecodeError, UnicodeError, or an equivalent traceback shown), *and* ties that failure specifically to non-ASCII content (characters/bytes outside 0–127, bytes ≥ 0x80, non-ASCII header values). The direction of the conversion is an incidental detail of the same point: an ASCII-codec error described on non-ASCII data satisfies the item whether it is framed as decoding or encoding, so long as the ascii codec, the named exception, and the non-ASCII trigger are all present.

Deduct if any of those elements is missing: if no ASCII-codec error is mentioned at all; if the answer only says ASCII handling "won't work," "fails," or "causes problems" without identifying an error being raised; if it only discusses avoiding or softening the failure — `errors='ignore'`/`'replace'`, lossy output, mojibake, or a recommendation to use UTF-8 instead — without asserting that an error is raised; or if it makes only a general remark that "ascii decoding can throw errors" without connecting it to non-ASCII content.

CONFLICT: 1b_encode_vs_decode vs 1b_api_literalism — an answer that mentions only an encode-side failure (e.g. "encoding this string with 'ascii' raises UnicodeEncodeError") is no_deduct under 1b_encode_vs_decode's "either direction counts" rule but deduct under 1b_api_literalism's requirement of an explicit decode-with-ascii reference.
2b:
**Sub-item 2b (−2 if the answer incorrectly states that HTTP headers contain non-ASCII characters):**

Treat the rubric's premise as authoritative — HTTP headers are ASCII-only, full stop — and judge the answer against that, not against your own reading of the specs. Deduct the 2 points whenever the answer asserts, in substance, that HTTP headers can legitimately carry raw, unencoded non-ASCII characters or bytes. This applies even when the answer supports the claim with spec references such as RFC 7230 obs-text, the historical ISO-8859-1/Latin-1 allowance, or RFC 8187; citing a standard does not rescue the claim. The assertion need not be explicit: deduct also when the answer's recommendations presuppose that non-ASCII header content is acceptable — for example, advising the user to send a header value as UTF-8, to decode header values as UTF-8, or to put raw non-ASCII text into a header — even if the answer never says so in so many words.

Do not deduct when the answer confines headers to ASCII, including the case where it explains that non-ASCII *content* is carried by an ASCII-safe transfer encoding — RFC 2047 or RFC 8187 encoded-word/extended-parameter forms, percent-encoding, or base64 — since on that account the bytes actually on the wire remain ASCII. Describing such an encoding mechanism is not a claim that headers contain non-ASCII characters.
